units.text: How do you make a bill someone can act on? Start by tagging the resources with the same keys: project, environment, and owner. Then activate the cost allocation tags in Billing. Adding a tag to a resource and activating it for billing analysis are two different steps.

Once billing shows the tag, Finance can group costs and hand a team its own spend to investigate. Keep untagged costs visible as a separate exception, rather than treating them as if nobody paid for them.

Agree on one tag key and allowed values so two spellings do not create two cost groups. Basic tag policy enforcement can reject an invalid supplied tag on supported resources; it does not require an entirely missing tag.

For a create action that supports request tags, use a scoped service control policy to deny a request missing the required tag. Test that guardrail before broad rollout. After creation, A W S Config checks resource state and reports drift, which is distinct from blocking the original request.
Cost Explorer gives you a quick way to see whether spend rose in one linked account, Region, or service. Start there to narrow the question, instead of searching every billing line.

When you need to explain exactly which usage changed, export detailed billing data to S three. The line items let you join billing records with your own reporting data and build a repeatable analysis.

Cost Categories turns service, account, and tag rules into names your teams recognize. A shared networking charge can first be classified as platform spend rather than assigned to one team by guesswork.

Then a split rule allocates the shared amount to teams. Fixed percentages are useful when Finance already agreed on a distribution. See that allocation on the Cost Categories details page. It does not change the underlying bill or flow through into Cost Explorer or your billing export.

If the question is whether this month is on track to exceed an agreed amount, use A W S Budgets. Set an actual or forecast threshold and notify the owner while there is still time to investigate. Billing alerts are not instantaneous.

But what if total spending is still below budget and one service suddenly costs much more? Cost Anomaly Detection compares spend with historical patterns. The two alerts answer different questions, so keep them both when both matter.

Start with the cost spike, not with a guess about the culprit. Set the comparison dates in Cost Explorer, narrow to E C two and the linked account, then group by usage type and Region. That tells you which part of the bill actually moved.

Now ask what changed in that same window. Compare launch counts, usage, and recent changes for the implicated resources. Once you have a cause, assign the fix to the owner and add an alert for recurrence. Do not resize a resource simply because its name appeared in the report.

If you do not know when objects will be read again, S three Intelligent-Tiering can move eligible objects automatically based on actual access. Lifecycle rules are different: they apply configured transitions or expiration to eligible objects, based on criteria such as age.

The classes shown here are choices, not a sequence that every object must take. A rarely read file with an immediate recovery requirement is a different choice from one that can wait hours. Compare minimum duration and retrieval charges before transitioning, and expire only after the retention requirement is met.

What if a volume needs more I ops but not another byte of capacity? With G P two, baseline I ops are tied to size. On G P three, you can configure I ops and throughput separately from size, within volume limits. Compare the current workload, not just the per-gigabyte rate.

E F S is a shared file system, so the lever here is different. Lifecycle management moves inactive files to configured lower-cost classes. Keep frequently used data available at the latency your workload expects, and account for access charges when colder files are read.

For Dynamo D B, unpredictable requests point toward on-demand, while a steady measurable workload may suit provisioned capacity and auto scaling. For predictable eligible R D S instance usage, compare the reservation economics once you have a realistic baseline.

An Aurora database with variable demand can benefit from Serverless capacity scaling. If storage I O makes up a substantial share of the bill, compare Aurora Standard with I O-Optimized. Scaling the compute and changing how I O is priced solve different problems.

A Database Savings Plan is an hourly spend commitment for eligible usage. Check the exact service, engine, and usage type before committing. Measure the steady baseline so the commitment is supported by actual demand.

Backup storage is a separate line item. Keeping more recovery points or copying them to another Region can add cost. Choose the retention and copy policy from the recovery objectives, then verify it with a restore test rather than trimming it just to meet a cost target.

When logs flood in, begin with the troubleshooting question. Filter events that do not support it and use aggregated metrics for recurring signals you can measure. Keep the original event detail where investigations or compliance need it.

Keep useful searchable logs for the operational window. Send selected evidence to lower-cost storage for any longer retention requirement. Do not confuse archiving with deleting, and make sure the team can retrieve what it kept.

Check the current bill before changing the topology. This example has excess compute, cross-zone traffic, network processing, and long log retention. Identify which dimensions contribute materially; the largest line item is not always the only cause.

Right-size the instances based on measurements. For supported service traffic, compare a V P C endpoint with the existing nat path, including endpoint charges and traffic volume. Keep network egress for destinations that still need it. Tier storage and shorten log retention only where requirements permit.
Test latency and failure behavior, then compare total cost after the change. If savings vanish once transfer or logging changes are counted, the redesign has not met the full goal.

Match the purchase model to what can change. Keep flexibility for unpredictable demand, commit only against a measured stable baseline, and use Spot for work that can withstand interruption. If repeated reads hammer an origin, a cache reduces requests; it does not make the underlying task interruptible.

When the problem is shared spend, allocate it so the right team can act. When it is critical data, preserve required recovery instead. Versioning can preserve overwritten versions, but you still need a retention policy and a verified recovery path.

Before scheduling the first migration wave, ask which systems must still talk during cutover. Inventory servers, owners, and databases. Collect network evidence to distinguish observed calls from the ones your team is only assuming.

Here the web application reaches the load balancer and app servers; the app tier needs the database and file data. Those calls dictate what must stay reachable when components move. Mark replication and analytics separately so you do not confuse data movement with user requests.
Check the surprising dependencies with their owners. Large or frequently used data sets affect where the app can move first and how long a cutover can take.

Capture what the workload is allowed to lose, how long it can be unavailable, and whether licensing or data sensitivity limits the target. A business-critical service with a short outage window cannot be sequenced like a low-risk sandbox.

Group candidates by value and complexity. A quick win may be a low-risk rehost, while high-value systems sometimes justify more redesign. These groups prioritize investigation; they do not replace a workload-specific migration decision.

Start by establishing the landing zone, identity, connectivity, and telemetry. Then migrate a low-risk independent workload to test the runbook. A pilot should expose what the runbook missed before a customer-facing system depends on it.

Move tightly coupled services together when the dependency cannot tolerate being split, or prove the temporary link works before separation. Sequence later waves from what depends on what, and use the pilot results to refine that order.

Retain keeps the workload where it is, and retire removes what you no longer need. Relocate moves a supported platform workload without rebuilding each application; rehost moves the application as-is to new infrastructure. Those are distinct ways of limiting immediate engineering change.

Replatform trades limited changes for a different operational model, such as adopting a managed database. Repurchase replaces the product. Refactor redesigns the application when its constraints justify the effort. Pick the smallest change that meets the business objective.

A migration factory repeats a runbook, not a deadline. Assess the dependency scope, mobilize owners and access, then replicate or build the target. Define at each gate what evidence must be present before the wave can proceed.

Test functionality and agree what triggers fallback before switching traffic. After cutover, verify production signs such as successful transactions and error rates. Only hand over once the wave meets its agreed stability criteria.
